metadata.title: Change in socioeconomic educational equity after 20 years of PISA: A systematic literature review
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study is a systematic literature review of quantitative analyses using PISA data, not an original analysis of PISA microdata. As such, it does not compute achievement scores, plausible values, or equity indices from raw student responses, and it does not apply PISA sampling or replicate weights in model estimation. Instead, it codes and synthesizes how included studies operationalized equity change (e.g., equality of opportunity via ESCS gradients/R-square or slopes; equality of outcome via dispersion/gaps; resilience via proportions of disadvantaged students reaching high performance; segregation via indices such as Duncan/dissimilarity). The review explicitly notes that the authors opted not to use weighting schemes across included studies and therefore treat the coded results as presented in the reviewed documents.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because this paper does not estimate cognitive achievement outcomes from PISA microdata; it synthesizes secondary findings reported in included studies and official OECD PISA reports. Missing-data handling is not reported because there is no original statistical modeling pipeline on individual-level PISA responses; the review’s coding procedure is based on whether included sources presented interpretable country-level evidence of equity change.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The review includes publications that report original quantitative analyses of PISA data on change in socioeconomic educational equity, requiring at least two PISA data collection points and English/Portuguese/Spanish/Russian/French text. Studies focusing on other equity types without socioeconomic equity were excluded; studies based on only one PISA wave were excluded. During screening, the authors further excluded full-text sources that did not discuss country-level change in equity with clear, readable evidence (e.g., missing objective cut-off criteria such as p-values or equivalent proxies, or missing explicit country trend statements).

The review protocol follows Petticrew & Roberts (2008) and PRISMA (Page et al., 2021), searching EBSCO, Web of Science, and Scopus, and updating the search in March 2024. It includes 33 original quantitative articles plus 5 official OECD PISA reports, covering PISA waves from 2000 to 2022 (and OECD comparisons using subject-rotated waves such as 2000–2009 for Reading, 2003–2012 for Mathematics, and 2006–2015 for Science). The synthesis finds no clear overall trend of equity improvement across participating countries, with substantial heterogeneity by equity dimension (opportunity, outcome, resilience, segregation) and by time frame. Limitations include reliance on how primary studies define and code “change” (often with weak or missing objective cut-off criteria) and the fact that the review does not re-estimate equity indices from microdata. data.outcome_summary: This paper is a systematic literature review (not an empirical ML study) examining how quantitative PISA-based research has assessed change in socioeconomic educational equity over roughly 20 years. The review protocol follows Petticrew & Roberts (2008) and PRISMA (Page et al., 2021), searching EBSCO, Web of Science, and Scopus, and updating the search in March 2024. It includes 33 original quantitative articles plus 5 official OECD PISA reports, covering PISA waves from 2000 to 2022 (and OECD comparisons using subject-rotated waves such as 2000–2009 for Reading, 2003–2012 for Mathematics, and 2006–2015 for Science). The synthesis finds no clear overall trend of equity improvement across participating countries, with substantial heterogeneity by equity dimension (opportunity, outcome, resilience, segregation) and by time frame. Limitations include reliance on how primary studies define and code “change” (often with weak or missing objective cut-off criteria) and the fact that the review does not re-estimate equity indices from microdata.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse by design because the article is a systematic review rather than an original empirical analysis. Consequently, there is no student-level dataset used for modeling, no ML training/evaluation, no plausible-values computation, and no country-level per-economy sample sizes reported for the review itself. The review’s “results” are coded qualitative/quantitative summaries of whether included studies reported positive/negative/no-change trends for equity indicators, rather than performance metrics from predictive models.
